answers.question: I haven't run for two weeks. Do I have to start again from the beginning? And is the 5K in four weeks still realistic?
answers.answer:
No, you don't need to start again from the beginning. Two weeks off costs you a little, not everything you've built since August. On Monday you drop back to 7 x 2 min run and 1 min walk, a session you handled at effort 6/10 on Sep 28. If that feels fine, Wednesday goes back to 8 x 2 min, and on Saturday you try 3-minute running spells for the first time.

Finishing the 5K on Nov 15 is realistic. Running the whole way is very unlikely, and I would not push for it. So far your longest unbroken run is 2 minutes, but the race will take you around 40 to 45 minutes of running.

Most new runners need eight or more steady weeks to close a gap like that. You have three training weeks plus race week. Rushing it is how new runners pick up niggles that stop them altogether.

A walk-run with walk breaks decided in advance, such as 4 or 5 minutes running and 1 minute walking, can get you round in about 45 minutes. Planned walk breaks are a race strategy, not a failure. Check the race's cut-off time, and keep running the whole way as the goal for a 5K in the new year.

new.analysis:
## How the week went
You did none of the three planned walk-runs Oct 12 – 18, and with your mum in hospital that was the right call. It is part of a pattern, though: you have done no running in three of the last five weeks. The good news is that your runs after the last break felt like effort 6/10 with no pain.

## Why the restart point
The plan picks up one step below your Oct 3 session, not at the beginning. Two weeks off takes a little edge off your breathing and legs. For a new runner the bigger issue is tendons and joints, which adapt slowly, so a gentle first week lets them catch up.

## Why every session stays easy
Three or four weeks before a race, experienced runners usually add race-pace work. That sharpening is for people who can already run the distance. Your job is different: make the running spells longer and spend more time on your feet, all at an easy effort.

## Run slower to run longer
On Oct 3 your heart rate sat almost entirely in zone 3, around 143, while you ran at about 7:40 per km. That pace works for 2 minutes but is hard to hold for 4 or 5. Slow the running spells until you could talk in short sentences, even if it feels like a shuffle.

## The road to Nov 15
You only move up a step when the one before felt like effort 6/10 or easier and nothing hurt. If a week goes sideways, you repeat it rather than skip ahead. Here is a rough outline, which we will adjust each week:

| Week | Running spells | Longest session |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Oct 26 – Nov 1 | 3 min, moving to 4 min, with 1 min walks | about 35 min |
| Nov 2 – 8 | 4 to 5 min, with 1 min walks | about 40 min |
| Nov 9 – 15 | short, easy sessions, then the race | 5K walk-run |

## Fitting it around your mum
When a planned day falls through, move it to the next free day, keeping a rest day between runs. Never squeeze two missed sessions into one. A shortened 15-minute walk-run still counts and keeps the habit going.
